title: SRE GPU maintenance and cluster recovery - runbook draft
content:
Status: DRAFT - working notes and steps for on-call to follow during GPU/node infra failures.

Purpose:
- Provide concise, actionable steps for SREs to recover from GPU hardware failures, perform safe node cordon/drain, add capacity, and execute cluster-level recovery if control plane parts are impacted.
- Keep guidance minimal for 1st responder; include escalation and post-incident checklist.

Scope:
- Applies to: k8s clusters running Redwood inference serving (hosted and dedicated), GPU node pools (NVIDIA A100/A30, AMD MI250), and on-prem racks managed by oncall SRE.
- Not covered: full on-prem hardware replacement logistics beyond handoff to data center techs (see HW-handbook link in linked artifacts).

Prereqs / quick checks (first 5 minutes):
1) Identify impacted cluster and node(s): kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady or look for GPU-annotated nodes with Ready!=True.
2) Check Redwood Console alerts: token-level latency spikes, model fallback events, and per-route errors.
3) Slack #gpu-failures and incident channel: announce "INVESTIGATING - cluster X node Y GPU failure" with brief facts.
4) Open incident ticket (if not already): tag SRE oncall, include cluster name, node id, control plane health, and hit count of affected pods.

Triage checklist (command snippets):
- Node health and kernel messages:
  kubectl describe node <node-name>
  ssh admin@<node-host> journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 | tail -n 100
  dmesg | grep -i nvidia -A50 || dmesg | grep -i gpu -A50
- Kube events and pod failures:
  kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -o wide | grep <node-name> || kubectl get events -n redwood-serving --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -n 50
- Device plugin state:
  kubectl -n kube-system get daemonset nvidia-device-plugin -o wide
  kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/nvidia-device-plugin -l name=nvidia-device-plugin --tail=100

If hardware (GPU) confirmed bad: GPU replacement workflow (remote-first):
1) Cordon the node immediately to stop new scheduling:
  kubectl cordon <node-name>  # mark unschedulable
2) Drain the node with graceful eviction where possible (preserve cache warm if serving critical traffic):
  kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=10m
  Notes: For latency-critical serving pods with local KV cache, prefer to use --pod-selector to target batch or training pods first. Communicate to product owners if graceful drains will cause transient capacity loss.
3) Verify pods evicted and re-scheduled to other nodes in the same pool with GPU resources:
  kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o wide | grep <pod-name-or-deployment>
4) If pods stuck terminating >10m: force delete and record stack traces in ticket:
  kubectl delete pod <pod> --namespace redwood-serving --grace-period=0 --force
5) Remove node from load balancers / gateway (if applicable) and update any external routing policies (Redwood smart routing may have pinned model variants).
6) Raise a hardware replacement ticket with vendor / datacenter and include: serial number, node id, last reboot time, journal logs excerpt, dmesg. Use template in confluence.

Physical replacement handoff checklist (on-prem):
- Confirm power-off procedure with site tech.
- Label node, document removed GPU model and serial.
- After replacement: verify driver/OCI compatibility and re-install device plugin and cuda drivers.
  sudo modprobe nvidia_uvm && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
  Verify: nvidia-smi shows expected GPUs.
- Uncordon node: kubectl uncordon <node-name>
- Observe pod placement and ensure that device plugin does not schedule pods until node annotated "gpu-ready=true" (we use an annotation gating step during onboarding - see onboarding-automation repo).

If cloud-based (GCP/AWS/Azure) GPU node replacement (quick path):
- Mark instance as unschedulable and cordon as above.
- For ephemeral worker pools, prefer to delete the instance and let autoscaler recreate it with same GPU type. Example: gcloud compute instances delete <instance-id> --zone=Z && verify node rejoins.
- For managed node groups, use provider CLI to replace the VM and watch node rejoin: aws eks update-nodegroup-version/eksctl delete nodegroup / recreate or gcloud container clusters resize / recreate node pool.

Node cordon/drain gotchas (lessons learned):
- Do NOT drain control-plane nodes unless instructed by platform oncall.
- Draining can cause spike in token costs if many models are reloaded — communicate expected cost/latency impact to product.
- Watch for stuck CSI or emptyDir volumes; use --delete-emptydir-data only when volumes are ephemeral.

Cluster recovery (control-plane impact) - immediate steps:
1) Identify control plane symptom: apiserver down, etcd quorum lost, controller-manager crashloop, inability to schedule across cluster.
2) Check etcd health (for self-managed etcd): curl -sS --cacert /etc/etcd/ssl/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:2379/health || ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=<ip:2379>
3) If etcd quorum lost: do NOT restart members blindly. Follow back-up restore runbook (link in linked_artifacts). Bring up a temporary etcd restore pod using snapshot and restore to a new cluster if needed. This is heavy; escalate to senior SRE.
4) If apiserver is overloaded (thundering herd from model restarts): identify offending controllers with top-like tools and temporarily scale down non-critical controllers (e.g., batch processors) and reduce admission controller policies.
5) If scheduler is healthy but nodes NotReady: investigate networking CNI and kubelet; check node's kubelet logs before rejoining.

Capacity add (quick scale for spike or replacement):
- Temporary fast path: scale out GPU node pool by N nodes via cloud provider, or trigger node pool autoscaler increase. Example (GKE): gcloud container clusters resize <cluster> --node-pool <gpu-pool> --num-nodes <target> --region <r>
- Ensure new node has kubelet tags and labels expected by serving daemonsets: kubectl label node <node> gpu-type=<type> && kubectl taint nodes <node> nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule (if used)
- Reconcile node labels/taints with deployments' nodeSelector and tolerations in redwood-serving namespace.
- Post-scale validation: run smoke tests that exercise generation endpoints and embeddings endpoints; check Redwood Console SLO panels for latency and error rates.

Automation reminders (add to runbook):
- Add automations to: detect repeated GPU ECC/thermal errors (journal logs), auto-cordon nodes with >=3 GPU errors in 10m, and create replacement tickets.
- Hook device-plugin health checks into alerting with runbook links.

Escalation matrix:
- Oncall SRE -> Senior SRE (if etcd, apiserver) -> Platform Eng -> Hardware vendor or Datacenter ops -> CTO on major outage affecting >50% capacity or >2 hour degradation.

Post-incident debrief quick template (to add to ticket):
- Timeline (first alert -> mitigation -> fix -> restore)
- Root cause hypothesis (hardware fault / driver / kernel / scheduling bug)
- Action items (driver pin, kernel upgrade, automation rule) with owners and due dates.
- Canned communications: short status note for product and customers.

Notes / TODOs for this draft:
- Add explicit commands for our internal cluster-provisioning tool (clusterctl alias) and device-plugin upgrade commands.
- Link to HW spare parts inventory and contact list for site techs.
- Add exact smoke test curl commands that validate token streaming and kv-cache warm paths.
- Add sample alert thresholds (GPU ECC rate, node restart rate) and PagerDuty escalation rules.

Example quick smoke test (curl):
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_KEY" -d '{"model":"rwd/stream-small","input":"hello"}' | head -n 20

Retention and change log:
- Keep runbook in Drive as working doc; once stable, move finalized version to Confluence and link here.
- Changelog (this draft): 2024-10-12 initial draft by Ava Chen; 2024-11-01 added cloud replace notes and escalation matrix (Marcus Li).

End of draft. Feedback welcome — add comments inline or ping oncall in Slack for urgent corrections.
